text.p: Centennial Coal Co Ltd, which suffered the largest percentage fall of any listed stock during Monday trade, said it was confident it had the support of investors.
Shares in the New South Wales steaming coal miner were at a two-year low of A$1.40 in late trade, a drop of 27 cents on the day or 16.2 percent.

"I think we have proved that we are good operators of coal mines and the market will recognise that and stick with us," managing director Bob Cameron told Reuters. "Obviously, we are a bit disappointed that it (the share price) has gone down."
The sharp fall in the share price to a level not seen since late March 1995 followed a slump in the company's half year profit result released last Friday.

Centennial's first half net profit slumped to A$1.1 million from A$2.67 million a year ago, with the company citing weak export prices and competitive bidding from miners in Indonesia and elsewhere in Australia.

"The climate has changed and things outside our control have hammered us," said Cameron, who noted that the company had met its prospectus forecasts since floating in August 1994 and that investors had strongly welcomed this.
The company produces 1.75 million tonnes of steaming coal annually from its underground and opencut mines throughout the state of New South Wales.
Two thirds of its production is sent overseas, hence the severe impact of lower prices on the company's balance sheet and share price.

South Korean energy firm Yukong Ltd is a five percent partner in the Charbon mine, while the Korean Electric Power Corp is one of Centennial's major buyers, along with non-utility customers in Japan such as steel mills, paper manufacturers, and textile firms.
Asked if Centennial could match the 1995/96 (July-June) net profit of A$4.94 million, Cameron said he did not want to comment specifically.

"But I would say that the (export) market will continue to be hard. The mines are going well. The local market, I think, is strong and probably stronger than it was in the second half of last year," he said.
"But the export market is still soft and it will be a while before returns start to improve. It will improve by the end of this calendar year."
Cameron said Indonesia had become a force to be reckoned with in the last few years and this along with more output in Australia had hurt the first half profit.

"I think they (Indonesia producers) have become a very strong competitor in export markets, more so than I think people envisaged a couple of years ago. Plus there is quite a lot of new supply in Australia, in the Hunter Valley (of NSW) in particular in the thermal market."

Cameron said Indonesia might not be a long term problem for Australian producers as the developing nation could face difficulties achieving the infrastructure needed to produce high quality export coal and would also face a growing domestic market which would be serviced as a greater priority.
